scenes.title: The Cartoon That Paid in Bitcoin

cues.text: This little USB drive holds more than half a billion dollars.
And it has two guesses left.
Get the password wrong two more times… and it destroys everything inside. Forever.
Go on. Try.
The man who owns it knows this. He's known it for years. And the drive is still sitting there… locked.
So what's on it? How did one forgotten password become one of the most expensive mistakes in tech?
And when a team of hackers offered to break it open… why did he say no?
This is the story of the drive that never forgets.
Meet Stefan Thomas. A programmer. Back in 2011, almost nobody had heard of Bitcoin. And Stefan made an animated video explaining what it was.
Yes. A cartoon. Like this one.
And for that video, he was paid seven thousand and two bitcoin.
Back then, bitcoin was worth almost nothing. So seven thousand of them? Pocket money.
But Stefan was careful. He put the keys to those coins on a special drive called an IronKey.
And the IronKey is not a normal USB stick. It's built like a tiny safe. Military-grade encryption. A secure chip inside. And one very famous rule.
Ten guesses. Get the password wrong ten times in a row, and the drive wipes its own secret key. The data is gone. No undo. No reset. No customer service.
So Stefan picked a strong password. He wrote it down on a piece of paper.
And then… he lost the paper.
At first, it didn't matter much. Bitcoin was cheap.
But then bitcoin started climbing. A hundred dollars. A thousand. Ten thousand.
And every time the price went up, that little drive got more valuable… and more locked.
So Stefan started guessing. His usual passwords. The ones he always used.
Guess one. Wrong. Guess two. Wrong. Three… four… five… six… seven…
Eight guesses. Eight misses.
Two left.
He told the New York Times: “I would just lay in bed and think about it. Then I would go to the computer with some new strategy, and it wouldn't work, and I would be desperate again.”
By 2021, the coins on that drive were worth about two hundred and twenty million dollars. And at bitcoin's peak, in October 2025? Close to nine hundred million.
So why not just… break it open? Plug it into a computer and try a million passwords?
Because the IronKey remembers.
Every wrong guess is counted inside its secure chip. Unplug it, wait a year, plug it back in… the counter is still there.
The chip is sealed under tough epoxy, built to resist exactly this kind of attack.
Even Kingston, the company that makes IronKeys today, said it couldn't help. No backdoor. No master password.
So it's impossible. Right?
Want to know if anyone ever cracks me? Subscribe. I'll wait. I'm very good at waiting.
Not quite. Because someone has pulled off something like this before.
Meet Joe Grand, a hardware hacker. In 2021, he took on a challenge from a man named Dan Reich.
Dan's crypto wallet, a little device called a Trezor, held about two million dollars in crypto. And he'd forgotten the PIN.
Dan and a friend had already guessed wrong twelve times. After sixteen, the wallet would wipe itself.
And every wrong guess made them wait longer before the next try.
So Joe didn't guess. He attacked the hardware itself.

He found that during a firmware update, the wallet copies its PIN into the chip's temporary memory. That memory is protected… but Joe hit the chip with a tiny, perfectly timed glitch in its power, and tricked it into letting him read it.
It took about twelve weeks of trial and error.
And then… the PIN popped up on his screen.
Two million dollars. Back.
But here's the catch. That trick used a flaw Trezor had already fixed back in 2017. Stefan's IronKey is a different, tougher machine.
Then, in 2023, a security company called Unciphered said it had done it.
Working with Wired, they took an IronKey of the same model as Stefan's, carved out its secure chip, dissolved the protective epoxy with acid…
…and ran about two hundred trillion password guesses.
It opened.
So they made Stefan an offer: let us unlock your drive.
And Stefan… said no.
Why would anyone say no to half a billion dollars?
Because, according to reports, he had already hired another team. And he'd agreed to give them a share if they succeeded.
So somewhere, maybe right now, someone may be trying to break into that drive.
Has anyone succeeded? As of today, there's no public confirmation that it's been opened.
And Stefan isn't the only one.

In Wales, a man named James Howells says he threw away a hard drive with around eight thousand bitcoin on it, back in 2013. It's buried in a landfill. He spent years in court trying to dig it up. In 2025, he lost.
One estimate, from the blockchain firm Chainalysis, suggested that up to one in five bitcoins may be lost forever. Forgotten passwords. Thrown-out drives. Owners who never told anyone.
So how do you make sure this never happens to you?
One. Use a password manager, so your brain isn't the only backup.
Two. Write down your recovery codes, and keep copies in two safe places. Not one piece of paper.
Three. Test your backup before you need it.
And four. Make sure someone you trust knows how to find it, if something ever happens to you.
Stefan called it a painful memory, and said he hopes others can learn from his mistakes. He said he was depressed for a few weeks… then decided to look forward, and keep building.
So here's my question. Two guesses. More than half a billion dollars. Would you try them yourself… or hand the drive to a hacker? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because next time, we're going to that landfill.
And I thought my sentence was bad.
Two guesses. I'll be waiting.
